narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other, passing in front of each other from our viewpoint and causing regular dips in brightness. The project samples TESS targets, applies statistical vetting to rule out noise and instrumental artifacts, cross-checks new candidates against six major variable-star catalogs to avoid duplicates, then runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal appears centered on the target star rather than a nearby object. So far, 323 candidates have passed this full pipeline. A machine learning model trained on thousands of labeled examples provides a second opinion on candidate quality, outperforming the rule-based baseline. The pipeline is transparent about its methods and honest about limitations: some candidates carry open caveats on their individual pages, and being listed here represents the end of what this automated process itself accomplishes.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars in orbit around each other, aligned so that from Earth's viewpoint they pass in front of each other. Each time one star crosses in front of the other, the total brightness of the system dips slightly. By studying the timing and depth of these dips, astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, masses, orbits, and temperatures.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' candidate on this site?
faqs.answer: A candidate is a star in TESS data that shows the statistical signature of an eclipsing binary. A confirmed candidate is one that has passed the automated pixel-level check, meaning the brightness dips appear centered on the target star itself rather than on a nearby object. 'Confirmed' here means it passed Star Vetter's pipeline - it does not mean the star has been scientifically verified or studied by other researchers.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?
faqs.answer: Star Vetter includes a machine learning model trained on thousands of labeled eclipsing binary candidates. It provides a second opinion on whether a candidate is real or noise, and it outperforms the rule-based baseline used in the vetting pipeline. However, it is not used to filter which candidates get checked - all candidates that pass statistical vetting and novelty checking go to the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score.

faqs.question: How does a candidate get checked?
faqs.answer: After a candidate passes statistical vetting and is confirmed to be novel (not already in six major variable-star catalogs), it undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This fully automated process examines the spatial location of the brightness signal to confirm it originates from the target star rather than a nearby object or instrumental artifact.

faqs.question: What happens if the orbital period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: The pipeline tests for period aliases by comparing the depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If the depths differ significantly, the measured period may be an alias - meaning the true period could be half the reported value, or related by another simple ratio. When this test flags an ambiguity, it is noted on the candidate's page.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Star Vetter lists each candidate's orbital period and eclipse depths as measured from the light curve. You can download TESS data for any target and examine the light curve yourself to check whether the reported signal is real and visually matches the description.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on Star Vetter?
faqs.answer: Being listed on this site is the end of what the Star Vetter pipeline itself does. The candidates are not automatically added to catalogs, sent for follow-up observation, or processed further by this project. Other researchers may choose to study any of them, but that is independent of Star Vetter's role.

faqs.question: Why should I trust these results?
faqs.answer: The pipeline applies multiple independent checks: statistical vetting rules out noise, a novelty cross-match against six catalogs avoids duplicates, and an automated pixel-level check confirms the signal is on-target. Additionally, a machine learning model trained on thousands of examples provides a second opinion that exceeds the performance of the rule-based approach alone. Results are presented transparently, with caveats noted where they exist, and the data and methods are open for anyone to verify.
